For God judges us based on our efforts much more than on the results – which are truly in His hands and not ours.
In any event, it is clear that practicing medicine is a wonderful merit, and an opportunity to help the many. Even if philosophically it may be argued that the results of our efforts are decided by God, a person who chooses such a profession has at the very least volunteered to make himself God’s messenger of healing to mankind, and that will certainly earn him much eternal merit. Much success in your chosen field!
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Hidden Light (Ohr HaGanuz) of Creation
questions.question: If God created light on the first day of creation, what is the idea that He created the heavenly bodies on the fourth? Where was the light coming from beforehand if not from the sun and stars?

answers.text:
Thank you for raising your interesting issue. The Talmud (Hagigah 12a) asks your exact question and gives two answers. The simpler answer is that God did in fact create the heavenly bodies on the first day, with His creation of the light. However, He did not yet arrange them in their respective places until the fourth day. In fact, the Midrash states that all the elements of creation were created on the first day of creation. Each was then put in its place within the earth or the cosmos on the appropriate day of creation (Bereishis Rabbah 1:19; see Rashi to Genesis 1:14,24).
The second answer given by the Talmud is that the light of the first day was not the light of the sun but a much greater and loftier creation – the original, unfiltered Light of Creation. With it, a person could see from one end of the world to the other. However, God foresaw that the world would eventually contain wicked people who were not worthy of enjoying such esoteric light. He therefore hid it away for the righteous in the World to Come.
We call this original Light of Creation the “Hidden Light” (ohr ha’ganuz) – as it was hidden away for the future. As is clear from the Talmud, it is not ordinary light but a spiritual essence too lofty for the physical world. It was the first entity God created outside Himself – with His very first utterance of “Let there be light.” This light is thus the part of creation which is so to speak “closest” to God – the most spiritual of all His creations (see The Science of God by Prof. Gerald Schroeder, pp. 161-165). Only the righteous in the World to Come will be able to bask in its glow. (The Sages state that this light was not hidden until after the first Shabbat of Creation (see Rashi to Bereishis 1:14).)
There is an interesting allusion to the existence of the Hidden Light in the wording of the Torah itself. The first light God created is called ohr, meaning “light”. By contrast, the verses discussing the fourth day of creation (Genesis 1:14-19) describe how God created the “me’orot” – which literally translates “from lights.” In other words, the heavenly bodies are not true light, but “from lights” – distant reflections of the true heavenly Light of Creation. They are energized by God’s true light, but they are covered and obscured by layers of physicality on the outside – so that they reflect God’s original light in highly attenuated form – enabling man to benefit from God’s illumination without being destroyed by its true inner radiance.
A deeper way of understanding the Original Light is as follows. We quoted above the Talmud’s statement that using the Hidden Light a person can see from one end of the world to the other. The idea is not that this light is physically brighter than today’s light. It is rather that it is so radiant and spiritually charged that it reveals reality as it actually is. It creates pure and unadulterated awareness – of everything in creation. It is the light of revelation – of shining God’s truth upon the world, revealing reality as it actually is and not as we finite beings perceive it.
Today, without this light, the truth is often hidden and God’s presence is badly obscured. We cannot even tell right from wrong. But the Original Light, a creation so holy and close to God, shines with complete and absolute clarity, leaving no room for falsehood or self-delusion. Today a person can act wickedly and either ignore it or somehow pretend his actions are justified. We can live with ourselves despite our flaws, almost pretending God isn’t really paying attention to us – since in our world of limited, physical light, we do not actually see God. However, in the Future World, with the true Light of Creation shining, there will be complete clarity – and knowledge of God. We will not be able to ignore or hide our faults. We will see our goodness and wickedness before us with complete lucidity.
The Talmud (Avodah Zarah 3b) writes as follows (slightly paraphrased): “In the End of Days, there will no longer be Gehenna. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, will take the sun out of its sheath and it will pierce. The wicked will be judged through it and the righteous will be healed through it.” Based on what we have explained, the meaning is that in the future, God will remove the covering from the true Light of Creation. (Recall that the heavenly bodies are referred to as “from lights.” They have the Light of Creation within them, but obscure it in layers of physicality. In the future, God will remove the “cover” from the sun – revealing His true light.) This intense light will bring complete clarity to the universe. The wicked will realize they have sinned and that absolute knowledge, with no way to hide from it, will destroy them entirely. Conversely, the righteous will now know just how good and worthy they were, and they will bask in their true and total knowledge of their closeness to God (as heard from R’ Yochanan Zweig).
(Some explain the Plague of Darkness in Egypt in a similar vein. The Sages tell us that while it was dark for the Egyptians, the Jews were bathed in light – and could even see where their Egyptians kept their valuables (Shemos Rabbah 14:3; Rashi to Shemos 10:23). Quite possibly, what God did was reveal His true light – at least to some small degree. This engulfed the wicked Egyptians, who couldn’t handle such unfiltered truth, in total darkness, while the worthier Jews benefited from this lofty light and could see piercingly – even discovering where the Egyptians placed their hidden treasures.)
(See Afikei Yam to Talmud Bava Metziah 86b, Nedarim 8b and Avodah Zarah 3a.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Sleeping Alone at Night
questions.question: Is there any problem with sleeping in an empty house?

answers.text:
Potentially. The Talmud (Shabbat 151a) writes that one should not sleep alone for Kabbalistic reasons. This applies if you live alone. Even if there are other people in the house but you have your own room, you should keep your door unlocked (unless that causes a yichud (seclusion) issue with a woman in the house). However, if light enters your room, the issue does not apply.
(Sources: Eishel Avraham O.C. 239; Mishna Berurah 239:8, Sha’ar HaTziyun 17; B’Tzel HaChochma IV 76.)
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Prayer Versus Accepting God’s Will
questions.question: If everything God does is for the best, why do we pray to God – asking Him to change our fate? Shouldn’t we accept that whatever God grants us is right for us and not ask that things be different? Isn’t prayer basically a rejection God’s will?

answers.text:
Thank you for your profound question. Even though we do accept that God gives us what is right for us, there are three primary reasons why we still pray:
(1) Many of the blessings we deserve in life God does not grant to us automatically and immediately. We must first pray for them to receive them. Our prayers open up the gates of Heavens and bring down the blessings we deserve.
(2) Even if we do not deserve a certain blessing, the very fact that we are turning to God in prayer and asking Him for it might make us worthier and more deserving of it. Thus, our prayers may grant us more than we would otherwise deserve.
(3) A variation of this is that sometimes even with prayer we do not actually deserve a certain blessing. Even so, God may respond favorably to our prayers simply because we turned to Him and asked for it. This is something you might be familiar with if you have small children – or remember from being one yourself. Sometimes, parents would normally turn down a request from their child – yet they might say yes anyway “because you asked so nicely” – teaching their child just how admirable it is when he speaks nicely and places his trust in his parents. God too is our loving Parent who responds to our wishes and may go so far as to change our decree for the better because of our sincere prayers.
Thus, even though we always accept that God gives us what is right for us, we pray for our needs as well – sometimes because the blessings we deserve only come through prayer, and sometimes because our very prayers make us more worthy of further blessings. All the same, we do accept that God knows what is best for us. Thus, if our prayers are not answered in the way we would like, our reaction must be to accept that God knows best, and what we’re asking for is clearly not truly right for us. But of course – viewing the other side of the coin – perhaps our prayers were turned down only because we didn’t pray hard enough for what we wanted – or improve ourselves in other ways to be deserving of such blessing. Thus, although we accept that God knows best, we can and should continue to pray for that which we feel we need.
Of course, at a point, we should probably adopt more of an acceptance mindset rather than a prayer mindset. If after years of heartfelt prayer God still does not grant us the blessings we desire, we should probably focus more on accepting God’s will – that He knows that what we want is simply not right for us – rather than refusing to accept that and continuing to forcefully pray. In any event, if our prayers are turned down, our attitude must never be that God is ignoring us and is insensitive to our needs. We must always approach prayer with the frame of mind that God might be saying no only because He knows what we want is not truly best for us – and that may well be for reasons only He understands.
This also touches on another fundamental question. If God knows our needs – even better than we do ourselves – why does He want us to pray to Him at all? Why ask God for what we think we need – which in fact might be wrong? Why not just leave it entirely up to Him?
The answer in a word is because God wants our prayers. He wants us to talk to Him and ask Him for our needs – not just leave it up to Him and never communicate with Him. He also wants us to go through the internal process of deciding what we feel we need and understanding ourselves better. I discuss this in a different response. Please see here for a further discussion.
Here are also a few nice articles on the general concept of prayer:
May God answer all your prayers for the good!
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Looking at Nails During Havdalah
questions.question: How come during Havdalah some people cover their thumb when the blessing is recited on the flame? I’ve also been told by others to hold the Havdalah candle as high as I want my future husband to be. Is there a Torah source for that?

answers.text:
The custom you’re referring to is not primarily to cover your thumb but to look at your fingernails – by folding down your right hand over your thumb and looking at your fingers. The technical reason for this is that when the blessing is recited on the flame, we must be close enough to it for the light to be usable to us – more specifically, to enable us to distinguish between a local and foreign coin (see Talmud Brachot 53b). If we can look at our hands and see the difference between our skin and nails, then we can be assured we’d be able to distinguish between the rather distinct coins of different countries as well. (Of course, it’s harder to tell this today with the house’s electric lights burning. But if you’re reasonably close to a multi-wick Havdalah candle, it’s safe to assume you’re alright.)
There are also Kabbalistic reasons for this custom. One of the best-known ones is that since your fingernails are constantly growing, beginning your week by looking at them assures you will have a week of growth. Also, for Kabbalistic reasons, you should look at your palm – and specifically not look at your thumb. The best way to do this is as we described above – curling your fingers over your palm, with your thumb tucked in, and viewing both together. Many then open their hand up, signifying that light will penetrate the darkness. They also turn their hand around while opening it and look at their nails once more from behind. (It’s also brought down not to look at the inner side of your fingers at this time, only the side with the nails.) This is all done with the right hand (although some repeat the same motion with their left).
This also applies to the person making Havdalah. Before smelling the spices (besamim), he should move the cup of wine from his right hand to his left, hold the spices in his right, make the blessing on them, and smell them. He should then keep the cup in his left hand while he blesses the fire and looks at his nails. This way, he too will look at the nails on his right hand. Afterwards, he returns the cup to his right hand and concludes Havdalah.
There is also a question if to look at your nails before the blessing on the fire is recited or right after. The more common custom is to look at your nails only after the blessing is said, although even better is to look at your nails both times. (This is what I do, but I only do the motion of opening my hand and looking at the back of my hand after the blessing, not before.)
Lastly, there doesn't seem to be any source for the notion of holding the candle as high as you want your future spouse to be. I know someone who used to meticulously hold the family’s Havdalah candle at about 5’11” from the ground. I commented to her that considering that she was already well into her twenties, her future husband has most likely already reached his full height, and it’s hard to believe that holding the Havdalah candle at a specific height will make the slightest difference! (Thankfully, she is long happily married – though to a man somewhat shorter than her target height.)
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch O.C. 298:3; Be’er Heitev 4; Mishna Berurah 9-11; The Radiance of Shabbos, pp. 138-139.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Marriage – Compatible Names
questions.question: I am God willing about to get engaged. My Hebrew name is ____ bat ____ and my fiancé’s is ____ ben _____. According to Kabbalah, is that considered a suitable match?

answers.text:
So long as you feel you are suitable for each other, you may surely marry. An engaged couple may request a blessing from a rabbi, but there is no reason to inquire if their names are compatible. One of the greatest sages of the past generation, R’ Yaakov Yisrael Kanievsky (1899-1985, known as “the Steipler”), wrote that we should not consider matching names for marriage. We should rather follow the exhortation of Deuteronomy 18:13: “You should be wholehearted with the Lord your God” – trusting that He will guide us properly and not basing our decisions for the future on bizarre mystical secrets. Further, people who claim to know how to determine such matters (certainly for a fee) are typically charlatans (Orchat Rabbeinu I 287).
See also Shu”t Mei’ein Omair (R’ Ovadiah Yosef), Vol. 12, p. 55 who similarly forbids this. Indeed, it’s been noted that based on such hidden “wisdom”, the names Abraham and Sarah are not compatible with each other – though I’m sure we can all come up with an Abraham and Sarah who together formed a wonderful Jewish home (and nation)!
If you read this further discussion (Hebrew), you will see that many scholars, even Kabbalists, consider the entire science of compatible names nonsense. Some Kabbalists do take it seriously but only view the matter as cautionary. Even if a man and woman do have incompatible names, it is at most an indication that they have different natural tendencies and predilections (as all married couples do). Yet people change throughout their lives, sometimes overcoming their flaws and sometimes acquiring new ones. Marriage does not depend on inbred qualities alone but on the person you have made yourself into throughout your years of life. And I think we can further add to this that even if a man and woman have somewhat different natures, a great part of marriage is bridging differences and building a close relationship despite that. If a husband and wife commit to each other and properly invest in their marriage, they can surely overcome any such mystical obstacles, even if they do exist. And anyway, as above, better to trust God and your own judgment – and choose a spouse for sound rational reasons, without searching for problems based on the nebulous world of Kabbalah.
(Note that some have a custom not to marry a woman with the same name as his mother or a man with the same name as her father. That is a separate issue and legitimate custom for those who observe it.)
answers.author: Aish.com Staff

questions.title: Why Does God Allow Animals to Suffer?
questions.question: Why do so many animals suffer in such terrible ways? A lot of this is caused by man – through such actions as destroying or contaminating natural environments, practicing agribusiness, and conducting medical research. Even in the natural world, animals often become food for predators. I understand that God might allow human beings to suffer as atonement for their sins or for their spiritual growth. But none of those reasons apply to animals. So why does God allow animals to suffer so?

answers.text:
Thank you for your important question. Unfortunately, there is no really satisfying answer to this. The basic response is that there is a fundamental difference between Divine Providence as it applies to man and as it applies to animals. People are granted a much higher degree of Heavenly protection. Every year on the High Holidays, we are judged whether or not we will be granted another year of life. Now there are complex philosophical questions precisely what is decided every year and its interplay with other factors. (For example, will a person’s individual judgment be affected by a national judgment (say, that God decrees a nation will suffer famine or war), can a person’s judgment be influenced by his fellow’s free will if his fellow decides to harm him, etc.) Regardless, we can state much more definitively that a human being will only die if God specifically willed it – or at least acquiesced to it.
Animals, however, are judged on an entirely different scale. God determines whether a species will survive or not, without regard for individual members of that species. Thus, if a fox wants to lunch on a rabbit – or a hunter wants to shoot a fox – whether or not the victim will survive depends more on skills of the pursuer than on God’s providential guard over the terrified prey. (This is the opinion of the majority of authorities – see for example Rambam, Moreh Nevuchim 3:17; Rabbeinu Bachya Genesis 18:19. (You can find a lengthy list of sources here.) I will add that Chassidic thought disagrees with this – seeing God’s providence as lovingly watching over every insect, every plant, and every leaf in creation. This, however, is not the opinion of virtually all early authorities.)
Sadly, the same is true if man’s cruel environmental practices destroy the world’s fauna (as well as flora) – or if his agricultural practices cause animals to suffer. God may intervene if we begin driving a species He chooses to preserve to extinction. But if we just harm or pain individual animals, God is much less likely to intercede. (This of course has nothing to do with a person’s judgment in Heaven for his heartless behavior – which will surely be quite harsh. We are only discussing whether or not God will protect animal life from the capriciousness of man.)
Thus, if people exercise their free will and act irresponsibly towards the environment, it will only harm people to the extent they deserve (although how a lot of the human suffering we witness in this world is “deserved” is generally beyond our understanding), while animals will be affected even though (of course) they have done no wrong. It is sad to see this in practice. But it is consistent with the manner in which God operates the world - and in many ways allows man's free will to ruin it.
As you also noted, a lot of the suffering animals endure in this world has nothing to do with man. The animal kingdom contains many carnivorous predators – whose survival depends on consuming animals lower down the food chain. And those predators themselves may find themselves food for yet higher predators. This is simply the way the world works. It appears inhumane, but it is natural and expected. And this raises a second question: Why did God create a world based on such cruelty? Surely, a perfect God could have come up with a more benign system – in which animals eat nothing but plants – and do so without multiplying endlessly and overrunning the earth!
The answer is that as a matter of fact this is not the way the world was originally created. From the time of Adam until the Flood, all animals were herbivorous, eating plants and nothing else. Only after the Flood and the fall of man did God permit both mankind and animals to eat meat (see Genesis 1:29-30 and 9:3). And if fact, that will again be the arrangement in the End of Days when the righteous will return to Eden. See this past response for a further discussion of this. And see also here regarding why God permitted the consumption of meat after the Flood.

questions.title: 10 Reasons I Love Being Jewish
questions.question: 10 Reasons I Love Being Jewish

answers.text:
From kidney donations to a 3,000-year-old prayer still recited today, here are 10 things that make being Jewish worth celebrating.
As we approach the High Holidays, I find myself reflecting on the past year, with all its highs and lows. I realize that many of my highlights stem from the joy and pride inherent in Jewish life. Here’s my list of ways I’m glad to be part of this crazy, unruly, occasionally maddening, but ultimately loving group called the Jewish People.
The Talmud notes that “All Jews are responsible for one another” (Shavuot 39a), and Jews continue to act on this today. When Hamas kidnapped 251 Israelis (not all of whom were Jewish) in 2023, Jews all over the world came together and prayed, lobbied, and demonstrated for their release.
Even in more prosaic times, being Jewish can sometimes feel like being part of one big family. Jewish students arriving at college know they can count on a warm welcome in campus Jewish organizations. Jewish travelers understand they’ll feel at home when they step into local synagogues, no matter how far away from home.
Being Jewish means you’re never really alone; you are linked to a wider Jewish community that cares about you and will step in to help, support, and celebrate together.
Judaism invented the weekend, the original TGIF moment at the end of the week when we can pause, take a breath, and switch our minds to a calmer way of being.
“Six days shall you work and on the seventh day you shall rest” (Exodus 34:21). Thousands of years ago, the Torah anticipated the breakneck business that so many of us experience today and proposed an antidote, mandating a day of rest each week for us to relax, reconnect, and remember that it is our humanity, not our productivity, which truly defines us.
Donating to charity is a key Jewish tenet that Jews have followed throughout our history, and still do today, at record levels. One study found that a large majority of American Jewish households regularly donated to charity at rates that far exceeded levels for other religious groups’ charitable giving.
Tzedakah, the Hebrew word for charity, gives us an insight into Jewish ways of giving. Unlike the English word charity, which comes from the Latin word caritas, meaning affection, the Hebrew word tzedaka comes from the root tzedek, meaning righteousness, justice. Whether you feel like it or not, Judaism places a demand to help others because it is the right thing to do, regardless of your feelings.
Jews lead the world in altruistic kidney donations. Revolutionized in the early 2000s largely by Jewish economist Alvin E. Roth - who would go on to win a Nobel Prize in 2012 - altruistic kidney donation seeks to solve the problem of a persistent lack of living kidney donors by encouraging people to donate a kidney to recipients who are unrelated to themselves. Over the past decade, altruistic kidney donation has become a major source of living kidney donations around the world, with Jews leading the way.
Israel leads the world in altruistic kidney donations, with far more donors per capita than in any other nation. In the United States, fully 17% of altruistic kidney donations are from Orthodox Jews, despite Orthodox Jews making up just 0.2% of the population.
It's incredible to realize that the Jewish traditions we enjoy today connect us to a chain going back thousands of years, anchoring us to the Jewish people. Enjoy matzah ball soup? Its roots trace back to Mount Sinai, when we were commanded to eat matzah instead of leavened bread at Passover (Exodus 13:6-7). Ever marveled at the beauty of Psalm 23, "The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want..."? King David wrote that timeless prayer over 3,000 years ago. Challah, Shabbat candles, apples and honey on Rosh Hashanah, reciting the Shema - these all link us to millennia of Jewish existence.
It’s a great responsibility and privilege to be the next link in the Jewish chain of tradition.
Judaism encourages us to debate, examine, and grapple with deep questions about life, to consider the opinions of others and formulate our own. The Talmud, Judaism’s core Jewish text, is filled with debates, commentaries on those debates, and even commentaries on the commentaries. Jews are encouraged to think deeply about our actions and our world, and to heed the insights of others who’ve similarly delved into life’s meaning.
To be Jewish is to be an eternal student, refining our understanding of the world around us. It means always questioning, learning, and growing.
The numbers are staggering: 22% of all Nobel Prizes ever awarded have been awarded to Jews. That’s 217 people, including 14 Israelis. This is despite making up just 0.2% of the global population. As your mother might say, what nachas (pride)!
The Jewish calendar is jam-packed with holidays that provide a framework for personal growth, and a reason to celebrate. From turning inward and evaluating our actions over the past year on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, to considering the way our ancestors resisted assimilation on Hanukkah, enjoying uproarious celebrations on Purim, celebrating freedom on Passover, and much more, Jewish holidays encourage us to think deeply about our lives and faith.
When it comes to our children, Jewish holidays give us beautiful ways to transmit our love for Judaism and create beautiful memories together.
Playing Jewish Geography is inevitable whenever Jews meet. “Where did you grow up?” “What summer camp did you attend?” “Saint Louis? Wow, do you know my Aunt Sadie?”
The goal underlying goal is to establish a Jewish connection, no matter how tenuous. Forget six degrees of separation; when it comes to Jews, those connections can shrink right down to two or three.
Jews are also familiar with the quintessential Jewish game of identifying which celebrities are Jewish. “Pink? She’s Jewish you know.” Ditto for Daniel Radcliffe, Rashida Jones, Daveed Diggs, and many others. That urge to make the Jewish connection partly stems from finding the common denominator in this sprawling Jewish community we call family.
Jewish communities have thrived throughout history. Even in the face of persecution, Jews have never stopped contributing to the world: inventing, creating, caring, and trying to make our communities and others a better place.
As Mark Twain famously wrote in his 1899 essay, Concerning the Jews:
If the statistics are right, the Jews constitute but one percent of the human race. It suggests a nebulous dim puff of star dust lost in the blaze of the Milky Way.

questions.title: The Prayer That Was Answered in Auschwitz
questions.question: The Prayer That Was Answered in Auschwitz

answers.text:
Doctors said Genna might never have children. Standing in Auschwitz, her body proved them wrong, in a way she never saw coming.
In July 2018, my husband and I joined a Heritage Retreats journey to Poland. Over several days we traveled to Auschwitz-Birkenau and to mass graves hidden deep in the forests. We cried, prayed, and recited Kaddish for Jews whose lives had been cut short.
Standing in Auschwitz, I was overwhelmed to find the names of my great-grandparents, Nochum and Chaya Rabovetsky, preserved in the archives among those murdered in the Holocaust. After mourning them, I made a promise: if they could no longer tell their story, I would live in a way that honored it. I recommitted myself to a life of Jewish observance and Jewish continuity.
Auschwitz-Birkenau, where more than a million people were murdered, the majority of them Jews, is impossible to process. The barracks, barbed wire, railroad tracks, and remains of the gas chambers confront you with a scale of destruction the mind can hardly hold. I'll never forget standing there with a group of Jewish young adults, many unable to hold back tears. We spread out, giving each other space to grieve.
As I looked around, I thought about everything stolen from them: weddings that never took place, children never born, grandparents who never lived to hold a grandchild, wisdom never passed down. Entire family trees cut down before they had the chance to grow.
One moment remains especially vivid. We entered a barrack with the prisoners' communal washing and toilet facilities. Our guide explained how inmates were stripped not only of their freedom, but of nearly every trace of privacy and dignity – and that prolonged starvation and brutal conditions caused many women to stop menstruating altogether, their bodies too depleted to function.
Prolonged starvation and brutal conditions caused many women to stop menstruating altogether, their bodies too depleted to function.
Prolonged starvation and brutal conditions caused many women to stop menstruating altogether, their bodies too depleted to function.
I couldn't shake one thought: how many women stood in that very place praying that if they survived, they'd one day become mothers – that they'd rebuild the families the Nazis were trying to erase? For countless women, that future never came. What happened to those prayers?
Standing near me was a young woman named Genna, with long red hair and striking eyes. What I didn't know yet was how personally this moment would hit her.
Since her teenage years, Genna had lived with a hormonal condition. She depended on medication to induce her cycle and had never experienced one naturally. Doctors had told her that having children might not be possible. Still, for as long as she could remember, she'd dreamed of becoming a mother and raising Jewish children.
Earlier in the trip, Genna had broken down crying, and I'd held her hand and spoken to her about Asher Yatzar, the blessing thanking God for creating the human body with the wisdom to function properly. Now, standing in the barrack listening to how starvation had stopped these women's bodies from functioning, she wasn't just hearing another horrific fact. She was thinking about women who'd dreamed of marriage and children, only to have it torn away -- and about her own fear that her body might deny her the same dream.
She began to feel faint. I watched her go pale and lose her balance; a friend helped her outside. Since so many of us had been physically overwhelmed that day, I assumed the moment had simply become too much for her.
A short time later, Genna felt an unfamiliar heaviness in her body and went to the restroom. There, for the first time in her life, without medication, her menstrual cycle had begun entirely on its own.
The timing was impossible to ignore. Minutes earlier, she'd been standing in Auschwitz hearing how starvation once silenced Jewish women's bodies, wondering if she'd ever become a mother. Then, in that very place, her body began working naturally for the first time.
It felt like a clear answer to the prayers of Jewish women who once stood in that same place pleading for survival, children, a future. Those prayers were not forgotten; Genna was their answer.
Jewish tradition teaches that no prayer is ever lost; God keeps count, even when we can't see the answer or know when it will come. A prayer can sit before God for decades before it finally becomes a blessing.
From that moment on Genna began saying Asher Yatzar blessing every day. She later described it as "the day of sadness that turned into a day of hope and belief."
Since that day in Poland, Genna has married and built the Jewish family she once feared she'd never have. In 2024, she and her husband Shachar welcomed her first daughter. "Even now, when I look at my two-year-old, there are moments I just stare at her in amazement," she told me. "I still can't believe I'm someone's mother."
A few weeks ago, she delivered her second child, another healthy girl.
"I think of the women whose dreams of motherhood were stolen from them. I think of the generations that never got the chance to exist," Genna told me. "I wanted is a family of my own. My motherhood is in honor of all those women who prayed for motherhood. I am the answer to their prayers. Having Jewish children is the biggest blessing and I can’t be more grateful for what I have been given."
Our journey through Poland was meant to honor the murdered by choosing life. Every Jewish child born, every family built, every generation that carries our heritage forward is proof they did not succeed. Genna's answered prayer is a reminder of an enduring truth: we don't know when an answer will come, or how. Sometimes it takes years. Sometimes generations. But we keep praying, and keep building, knowing that no prayer is wasted.

questions.title: How to Become More Emotionally Connected to Yourself, Your Spouse, and God
questions.question: How to Become More Emotionally Connected to Yourself, Your Spouse, and God

answers.text:
Simple ways to feel closer to your spouse, yourself, and God this Elul, no big gestures required.
Have you ever been in a room full of people yet felt alone? Or sat next to your spouse yet felt miles apart? Or stood in synagogue, saying words you've said year after year, wondering, Does God even hear me?
Loneliness isn’t the absence of people; it's the absence of emotional connection. It's commonly felt in marriage, within yourself, and in your relationship with God.
We give energy to our jobs, children, communities – even our phones. Then at 10:30pm we turn to our spouse and ask, "Okay, what do you need?" Our prime time should be given to our spouse, not our leftover energy.
Preserve energy for your spouse by saying no to others during the day, delegating tasks, or decreasing expectations of yourself. (Aka dinner can be plain rice and simple chicken, nothing fancy.)
Then, when you’re actually in front of your spouse, make a conscious choice to put down the phone and give them a few minutes of undivided attention. Don't just ask them how their day was -- go a drop deeper. Ask them the hardest part of their day, the best part of their day, or what's been weighing on their mind lately. When they answer, don't jump to fix it; just listen, validate, or offer a hug.
Your spouse wants your physical presence and needs your emotional energy as well.
You can become a stranger to yourself. You know you need sleep but you keep going. You need friendship but you're too busy to call. You need quiet but you immediately reach for your phone.
You distract yourself, overeat, or scroll, anything to avoid sitting quietly enough to hear what's happening inside.
How am I actually doing? What am I pretending doesn't bother me? What part of myself have I silenced because I'm afraid of disappointing someone?
Emotionally disconnecting from the self includes denying yourself things that make you feel alive. Make sure to listen to your inner voice and fill your bucket.
Give yourself five minutes of true quiet each day -- no phone, no music, just you. Notice what surfaces when you stop filling the silence.
Do one thing because it makes you feel alive, not because it's productive or expected of you. A walk, a hobby, a few pages of a book.
There have been times I've rushed through prayers so quickly I literally swallow my words. And then I finish and think: What just happened?
I prayed, but where was the connection? The Hebrew month of Elul is an opportune time to bring God into your daily life.
Make prayer personal. Use your own language and wording to tell God what you're worried about, grateful for, struggling with, and hoping for, as if you're speaking to someone who truly knows you.
Look for the small moments of Divine providence. Recognize that serendipity is God's guiding hand in your life. Recognize the small moments of kindness, beauty, and blessing. The more we notice, the more connected you feel.
One minute of gratitude, filling in a gratitude journal, or a heartfelt "Thank You" to God for help, can turn an ordinary moment into a relationship. Even one small step in the right direction can bring change and connection.
The month of Elul gives you a beautiful opportunity to rebuild your connection with your spouse, with yourself, and with God.
Perhaps that is why Judaism gives us three central practices for this time of year: teshuvah (repentance), tefillah (prayer), and tzedakah (charity).
Teshuvah reconnects you to yourself. It asks us to stop, look inward, and honestly consider who you have become and who you want to be. It’s a recalibration to get recentered with your soul, your true inner self.
Prayer reconnects you to God. It reminds you that you are never truly alone -- and that you can turn to Him with your worries, gratitude, hopes, and questions, any time, day or night.
Tzedakah reconnects you to others. It moves you beyond yourself by reminding you that you are part of something larger than your own life.
This Elul, take one small step towards strengthening your most important relationships, with your spouse, with yourself, and with God.

questions.title: China and the Jews: Two Ancient Civilizations, One Unlikely Friendship
questions.question: China and the Jews: Two Ancient Civilizations, One Unlikely Friendship

answers.text:
A Chinese teenager falls in love with Fiddler on the Roof and converts to Judaism. Acupuncture leads a burnt-out Jewish woman back to Judaism. Coincidence -- or something more?
The daughter of Holocaust survivors, Schwarcz had grown up in Communist Romania in a family shadowed by losses nobody talked about. Her mother had lost a husband and child in the Holocaust; her father had lost his wife. Yet the past remained largely unspoken.
Vera became fascinated with “the other.” She learned Mandarin, studied Chinese history and eventually headed to Peking University as a Far East scholar.
One travels light when relocating halfway around the world. But for reasons she could not quite explain, she brought along a book by Elie Wiesel about the Holocaust.
When Yom Kippur was around the corner, Schwarcz was overtaken by an impulse. She had no intention of fasting on the holiday but she decided that Tiananmen Square and the Cultural Revolution unfolding around her could wait. She would spend that day in her apartment reading Wiesel.
As part of her research, she was gathering oral histories from Chinese people who had suffered terribly during the Cultural Revolution. Something unexpected began happening.
“I found they were talking to me so openly about their horrible experiences,” she later recalled. “I realized I was unconsciously carrying languages and stories about national suffering and the Chinese were picking that up.”
Schwarcz had gone to China to study another civilization. Instead, China began turning her attention toward her own family’s ancestral trauma.
“There is something about Chinese culture that sends us back to ourselves,” she observed.
Eventually, Schwarcz became a distinguished historian of China, writing Bridge Across Broken Time: Chinese and Jewish Cultural Memory, a book that considers how traumatic memory is transmitted and healed in two ancient civilizations. Today she lives in Jerusalem as an observant Jew and feels that her immersion in Chinese culture ultimately led her home.
“I took the journey to Jewish memory and Jewish culture and observance through my China studies,” she said.
Her journey may sound extraordinary, but look closely at the encounters between these two ancient civilizations and something curious begins to emerge. It has happened again and again.
Hu grew up in Tianjin, China, in an atheist family. His unlikely journey toward Judaism began, of all places, with Fiddler on the Roof.
The musical captivated him. He was struck by Tevye’s ongoing conversation with God and by a question at the heart of the story: What happens when an ancient tradition encounters a rapidly changing world?
Eventually Hu moved to New York where he was drawn to explore Judaism in Jewish homes and communities. He became fascinated by Daf Yomi, the worldwide practice of studying a page of Talmud each day.
The English was difficult for him, so Hu turned to artificial intelligence to help render the material into Mandarin. He began learning Talmud in Chinese.
Hu compared the Talmud with the Analects of Confucius. Both preserve teachings, conversations and debates among sages, allowing later generations to enter into an ongoing dialogue rather than simply handing them a list of conclusions.
What started with Fiddler on the Roof has led him to convert to Judaism.
Zane is ethnically Chinese. His great-grandmother was once a wealthy Shanghai socialite married to a silk producer. In the late 1940s, she happened to be travelling outside China when the Communist takeover closed the country.
Her five children, including Zane’s then-five-year-old grandfather, remained behind.
She was unable to regain entry to China. She tried everything; nothing worked.
Desperate and eventually broke, she emigrated to New York, where the former heiress worked as a housecleaner. Later she found employment with a legendary Jewish family: the Grossingers of Catskills fame.
Years passed. When China eventually reopened to the West, she located her five children, now adults with families of their own.
The Grossinger family sponsored all her descendants, bringing family members to the United States, including the child who would become Nicholas Zane’s mother.
“A Jewish family’s act of grace would transform the trajectory of the Zhang family,” Zane later wrote, “and our lives would never be the same.”
At 15, Zane was attending an Anglican boarding school in Britain. Having grown up in Hong Kong, he had never met a Jewish person, yet he became engrossed in Jewish history.
The stories he had heard had left their mark. He became fascinated with the historical relationship between Chinese and Jews. He researched Jews in China, wrote books on the subject and became a public advocate for greater understanding between the two peoples.
Bring the Jewish and Chinese worlds together and people discover pieces of themselves in the other.
Bring the Jewish and Chinese worlds together and people discover pieces of themselves in the other.
Bring the Jewish and Chinese worlds together and unexpected things seem to happen. People discover pieces of themselves in the other. Kindness crosses cultures and reverberates through generations. A journey toward one civilization somehow leads a traveler deeper into the other.
Perhaps these are simply beautiful coincidences, but there are so many of them. Looking backward, the coincidences begin to resemble a pattern.
There was Morris “Two-Gun” Cohen, a rough-and-tumble Jewish immigrant whose intervention on behalf of a Chinese restaurant owner in Canada helped establish his reputation in the local Chinese community. Cohen eventually became involved with the Chinese nationalist movement and Sun Yat-sen. His unusual Chinese connections would later be leveraged to help secure China's cooperation regarding the establishment of the State of Israel.
Two-Gun Cohen, in the white suit, seated with President Chiang Kai-Shek on his right
There were the thousands of Jewish refugees who found sanctuary in Shanghai during the Holocaust. Among them was violinist Ferdinand Adler. China helped save his life; Adler, in turn, taught Chinese students to make music. One of those students, an orphan, went on to a career in Shanghai’s musical world. Generations later, their families would reconnect, the children piecing together a story that had begun long before either of them was born.
The Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, encouraged efforts to bring Jewish sources to Chinese readers and saw value in building bridges of understanding.
That interest continues to surface in contemporary Jewish life. Today, a Chinese reader can open a Chinese edition of Psalms published by Koren, containing the Hebrew Psalms, a simplified-Chinese translation and a Chinese translation of Rabbi Jonathan Sacks’ commentary. Its translator, Aaron Waldman, was born in Tianjin and later made aliyah, becoming a Torah scholar in Israel.
At Yeshiva University, the Chinese-Jewish Conversation was created to place these two civilizations into sustained dialogue. Its programs explore questions that have occupied both cultures across the centuries: education and family, classical texts and their transmission, tradition in confrontation with modernity, and the complicated relationship between homeland and diaspora.
Why does this conversation keep resurfacing? Perhaps because Jews and Chinese are similar enough to recognize something in one another, yet different enough to see things in each other that we cannot always see in ourselves.
Jewish and Chinese civilizations are not interchangeable. Their theologies, histories and cultural assumptions differ profoundly. Yet both are ancient civilizations that have carried an intense relationship with their past into the modern world. Both have traditionally emphasized learning, family, transmission between generations and reverence for foundational texts and teachers. Both have wrestled with the question of how to preserve a distinctive civilization through enormous historical upheaval and into a rapidly changing modern world.
Sometimes similarity creates recognition. Difference can provide something equally valuable: perspective.
Put two slightly different lenses together and something else becomes possible: depth perception. Binocular vision.
I became religious in my early twenties through Aish. A few years later, serious health problems overwhelmed me and I gave up observance. Searching for help, I turned to Traditional Chinese Medicine and underwent acupuncture treatment for several years.
I didn’t go to an acupuncturist looking for a route back to Judaism, but something happened. The treatment opened something in me and, slowly and unexpectedly, I found myself returning to Jewish observance. I ended up back at Aish, reawakening my love for Torah.
I subsequently began studying Chinese wisdom, fascinated by the points of resonance I encountered between Jewish and Chinese ideas. Over the years, I collected sources exploring concepts of balance and flow, water and wisdom, cycles and time, the cultivation of character and the relationship between Heaven and human conduct.
Years later, after working in antisemitism advocacy, I found myself longing for another kind of Jewish activism. Fighting hatred is necessary. But I wanted to spend some of my energy building something beautiful.
Then I saw an online interview featuring Chinese supporters of Israel, including a young woman who was both Chinese and Jewish.
I was mesmerized. Suddenly the pieces I had been collecting for years pointed toward something larger: What if Jewish advocacy didn't consist only of fighting our enemies? What if we also went looking for friends?
That question led to the creation of the Chinese-Jewish Exchange, an initiative of the Canadian Antisemitism Education Foundation.
The project grew from a simple recognition: again and again, encounters between Jewish and Chinese people have set unexpected things in motion.
A daughter of Holocaust survivors travels to China and discovers the unspoken Jewish memory she has carried within her. A Chinese teenager encounters Fiddler on the Roof and eventually finds his way to Orthodox Judaism. A Jewish family’s kindness to one Chinese woman reverberates through generations. Traditional Chinese Medicine brings a struggling Jewish woman back to Torah.
In each case, the encounter does more than introduce one culture to another. It awakens something. One civilization becomes the unlikely lens through which a person sees more deeply into the other, and sometimes more deeply into themselves.
The bridge between the Jewish and Chinese worlds has been quietly forming for generations, built through sanctuary, scholarship, gratitude, curiosity and kindness. Most of its builders did not know that they were building anything at all.
Perhaps our task now is to recognize the friendship that has been taking shape all along and to stop leaving its future entirely to chance.
The Chinese-Jewish Exchange, an initiative of the Canadian Antisemitism Education Foundation, is preparing programs and a free heritage display for Jewish Heritage Month and Asian Heritage Month in May 2027. We invite individuals and organizations to help bring the display to synagogues, schools, libraries, community centres and other public spaces. To learn more or become involved, visit The Chinese-Jewish Exchange.
answers.author: Ed.D.

questions.title: Getting Started
questions.question: I am married to a non-Jew. I swing back and forth between "doing" the traditional things and then not doing anything at all. As a Jew, I have decided to focus on Judaism in my graduate program. However, this summer I would like to begin my studies on my own. I can read and write Hebrew pretty well. In your opinion, what is the best way to get started? Should I begin with the Talmud? I continue to come back to missing the traditions, and need to know how to begin and how to stay on course. Where do I start?

answers.text:
In general, where should you start?
Believing in God is the primary commandment in Judaism.
Who is God?
God is the Creator of the world who gave the Torah and its commandments to the Jewish people at Mount Sinai. (See this article.)
A good way to bring that concept into your life is through prayer. Open your heart to Him and He will surely help. As it says: "God is close to all who call sincerely" (Psalms 145:18).
The best way to learn about Judaism is to live near a Jewish community which has adult education programs, rabbis you can talk to one-on-one, Shabbat hospitality programs, etc.
If that is not an option, then try Torah education websites, such as Aish.com. You should get a basic Jewish library started in your home. While commuting or cooking, you can also listen to audio lectures from the thousands of titles available at aishaudio.com.
If you are interested in trying out one-on-one Jewish learning, I recommend signing up at J-Inspire. Any subject can be learned, by phone or in person, at a time that's good for you. This service is absolutely free.
Also, it is very important to attend a Discovery seminar. That frequently can make a big jump-start, by providing a framework and overview of the entire gamut of Jewish history, philosophy, and answering the questions, "Why Be Jewish," "Does God Exist," and "Is Torah True?" For more info, go to aish-international.com/programs.
Best of luck and let me know how it goes!
answers.author: Aish.com Staff

questions.title: Adam’s Sin and the Decree of Death
questions.question: The Torah states that on the day Adam would eat of the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge he would surely die (Genesis 2:17). Yet although he was punished when he sinned, he didn’t die on that day, but lived hundreds of years longer. Am I missing something?

answers.text:
It’s an excellent question. There are several answers to this, most of which are variations of a single theme. To explain, we need to first have a deeper understanding of Adam’s sin.
Before Adam and Eve ate of the Tree of Knowledge, they were both spiritually and physically perfect. Man had no Evil Inclination. He had no inner desire for evil. The drive for evil was an external force, embodied in the Serpent, which attempted to lure man to sin. But man himself was wholly pure. His physical side was nothing other than a perfect reflection of his spirit.
As a result, before the Sin, man had the potential to live forever. His body did not contain the decaying influence of the Evil Inclination. His physical side had the same potential as his soul to be wholly perfected and to exist eternally. As the Kabbalists explain, had Adam and Eve passed their test and not eaten of the Tree of Knowledge, they would have afterwards eaten of the Tree of Life – to live eternally with God in Eden.
Once man sinned, however, evil became a part of his psyche. The Tree of Knowledge gave him an intimate knowledge of – and desire for – evil. Man’s evil inclination was no longer an external Serpent, but a part of his very soul. Man became a confused mixture of good and evil, the good only attaining ascendancy after the utmost of struggles. And man would never be fully secure in his spirituality. As high as his soul might strive upwards, his body would drag him down. He would never be entirely free of his physical wants and desirous nature.
As a result, death was a necessary part of man’s existence. Man could now never entirely perfect himself. His body was simply too corrupt for full rectification. It would have to die and decay – only to later be recreated in a higher state at the Resurrection, at which point – if it is worthy – to live forever (Derech Hashem I 3:9).
Based on the above, many of the commentators to the Torah explain that the punishment of death decreed on man did not mean to say Adam would literally die right then, but at that point he would be liable to death (Targum Yonatan, Ramban, Rabbeinu Bechaye, Chizkuni, Radak and many others), or that because of his imperfections death would now slowly overtake him (Malbim, also brought in Ibn Ezra 3:8). He would now be a finite being which would ultimately decay and die. Likewise, in Adam’s decreed punishment God tells him “for you are earth and to the earth will you return” (Genesis 3:19). His body was now corrupt, resembling the earth it derived from. Man was destined die.
Another interesting answer appears in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 19:14). Psalms 90:4 states: “For a thousand years in Your eyes are as yesterday which has passed.” By God’s standards, a “day” is a thousand earth years. Thus, in fact, Adam, who lived till 930, did die on the same “day” he ate of the Tree.
A final suggested answer is that Adam did in fact deserve to die right then, but because he repented God lessened his punishment and he lived much longer (Ibn Ezra 3:8, based on several Talmudic references to Adam’s repentance).
See here for a further discussion of Adam’s sin and its ramifications. See also this section for a much deeper treatment of the topic.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Prayer at Graves of Righteous
questions.question: I often receive emails from different organizations offering that a rabbi will pray for me at this or that great rabbi’s grave. Does it really make a difference where one prays? Isn't praying to a dead rabbi for salvation practically idolatry?

answers.text:
It’s a very important question. The notion of praying at the graves of the righteous is well-established. The Talmud tells us that Caleb, one of the spies sent to inspect the Holy Land, separated from the rest of the group to visit the Cave of the Patriarchs (ma’arat ha’machpailah) in Hebron. He prostrated himself before the cave and said to them “My fathers, plead for mercy for me that I be saved from the evil designs of the spies” (Sotah 34b).
Elsewhere the Talmud mentions a custom to visit a cemetery during times of calamity, such as a drought. The reason, according to one opinion in the Talmud, is so that the dead will ask for mercy for us in Heaven (Ta’anit 16a).
It has likewise been a Jewish custom all throughout the ages to consider the graves of the righteous (kivrei tzaddikim) places of pilgrimage, and to visit there and recite Psalms and prayers. Hassidim even leave notes (kvitlach) by their Rebbe’s grave.
As you point out, though, this must be understood correctly. Praying to a deceased person rather than God is idolatry. He cannot help you, no matter how great he was in his lifetime. What he might be able to do is intercede in heaven on your behalf. Thus, when a person prays at a grave, he should either have in mind that the righteous person (tzaddik) help bring his prayers to God, or even better, he should pray directly to God that He help him in the merit of the tzaddik buried here (Mishna Berurah 559:41, 581:27).
That being said, it may well be more effective to openly and sincerely pray to God for your needs yourself, rather than asking some great rabbi to do it for you. God gives us challenges and hardships in life so that we’ll turn to Him and improve ourselves – rather than that we find a great person to take them away for us.
answers.author: Aish.com Staff

questions.title: Praying in English – God’s Name
questions.question: I say the prayers in English because I’m too unfamiliar with Hebrew. Can I use the terms “God” and “Lord” for God’s name – as my prayer-book shows? Or are they not accurate translations

answers.text:
English terms like God and Lord are not true names of God and do not truly and accurately translate the Hebrew words for His name. Thus, it’s proper that even when you pray in English that you say God’s name in Hebrew. The main terms used are “Ado-nai” – which implies God’s infinity and mastery over all, and “Elo-him” (or “Elo-hainu”) – which describes God as all-powerful and the One who controls the entire universe. Note that these names should not be pronounced except during prayer or when quoting complete verses in the Hebrew.
It’s a good idea to buy the ArtScroll Hebrew-English siddur. (See here for buying choices.) It not only has a very accurate translation, but it can be used to help you slowly transition to praying in Hebrew. (Note that ArtScroll recommends saying God's primary Name in Hebrew, as Ado-nai, but uses “God” for the other names.)
See this article for further explanations of God’s names.
(Source: Teshuvot V'Hanhagot by R' M. Sternbuch, I 128.)
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Why Can't God Just Reward Us?
questions.question: I recently read an Aish article which explained quite cogently why God cannot simply reward man and place him in the World to Come. The basic reasoning is because people would be shamed by receiving something they did not earn. Receiving something for nothing does not give a person the good feeling of achievement and developing a relationship with God – which is what his share in the World to Come is built on, but it is an embarrassment (“nahama d’kisufa”). And therefore, God had to create this world of challenge, where we must overcome obstacles to get closer to God – in spite of all the pain and suffering this world contains, with so many people sinning and failing to get closer to God. My question is that I still don’t understand why God had to do things this way. Isn’t God all-powerful? God created us as people who cannot enjoy unearned reward, so He had to make us suffer through this terrible world first. But why couldn’t God just as easily have created man differently – as beings who can enjoy reward for nothing? Or perhaps God could have created a universe which has no notion that unearned pleasure is embarrassing? Then God could have put us straight in the World to Come! I mean, can’t God do everything?

answers.text:
Thank you for your profound question. You are probably referring to this article.
The answer may well go beyond what man is capable of fathoming, but I’ll offer you what I believe the response is.
Your question is based on your assumption that God can do everything, therefore why didn’t He simply make a different type of world. I’ll answer by posing a similar hypothetical question. Could God have created a world which has a Torah with different laws in it, in which, say, murder is a mitzvah? The answer is no, but this does not indicate a limitation on God’s power. A God who can literally do everything cannot create a world where murder is a mitzvah.
The reason for this is because there are certain truths in the world which are just realities, axioms of existence which cannot be altered. Murder is wrong not because God arbitrarily chose to give us such a law, but because it is intrinsically wrong. Nothing can change that, not even God, so to speak. Nor for that matter can God create a rock He cannot lift. This again does not mean God has a limitation, just that by definition such a rock cannot exist.
The same is true regarding the notion of reward and punishment. God could not have created a world in which God can “reward” us for free, in which human beings could enjoy the World to Come without ever having had to earn it. This is simply part of the reality of existence. A person only feels a sense of existence when he has made himself worthy and has developed a relationship with God. There is no such thing as experiencing a sense of reality for free. And that is not something God can change. It is as true as God and His Torah themselves.
Thus, to the extent we can understand, for the universe to be meaningful, God had to create a world of reward and punishment. Man would have to be challenged between good and evil. He would only come closer to God by overcoming those challenges and choosing good. Sadly, not everyone passes this challenge, but this is the only paradigm God could have used to create a universe.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Items Doomed to God
questions.question: I’m trying to make sense out of Leviticus 27:28-29. It seems to state that all items doomed to God, whether people, animals, or fields, may not be redeemed. They are most holy to God and must be destroyed or put to death. Does this mean that if a person dooms someone else to God he must be killed? Can we do this to anyone we don’t like? Perhaps this is why the judge Jephthah killed his daughter.

answers.text:
You are right that those verses appear quite shocking on simple reading. However, they are much more understandable based on the interpretations of the Sages.
Before beginning, I will note that according to the Sages the subjects of the two verses are somewhat different. We will therefore explain each one separately below.
Verse 28 reads as follows:
However, any doomed item which a man dooms to God of anything that is his, whether a person, animal, or the field of his heritage, may not be sold and may not be redeemed. All doomed items are holy of holies to God.
There is some debate in the Talmud (Erchin 28-29) regarding the precise meaning of the verse, but the principles are fairly well agreed upon. We can “doom” objects to God either by consecrating them to the Temple or to the Priests. When we do so, they become Temple or Priestly property. We may only consecrate that which belongs to us – whether our land, house, movables, animals or slaves. (This is the intent of the “person” mentioned in the verse; Talmud Gittin 38b, Erchin 28b.)
What does the Temple do with property consecrated to it? An animal fit for a sacrifice will be offered to God. Anything else will generally be sold by the Temple treasurers and the proceeds will go to the Temple treasury. (The owner himself can redeem what he consecrated by adding 25% to its appraised value.) All of the above is basically the subject of Leviticus 27.
Verse 28 discusses items consecrated to the Priests. Such items may not be sold by the Temple custodians and may not be redeemed by the donor (“may not be sold and may not be redeemed”). Rather, they become permanent Priestly property, divided up among the Priestly family on duty at the time the gift is dedicated. (Once the Priests divide them, they have no sanctity and can be used for ordinary household use (Talmud Erchin 29a).)
(The final phrase of the verse appears to refer to items consecrated to the Temple – which so become “holy of holies.” The precise interpretation is discussed by the Talmud (Erchin 28-29).)
Verse 29 is unrelated. It reads as follows:
Any doomed item which has been banned from mankind shall not be redeemed. It shall surely be put to death.
What is the meaning of this cryptic, ominous verse? There are two opinions (both appearing in Talmud Erchin 6b):
(1) The “doomed item” of the verse refers to a person (the Hebrew gives no indication if a person or object is intended). The “doomed” person is one whom the courts have condemned to death – and as a result, is banned from mankind. If a person vows to donate his worth to the Temple (see e.g .Leviticus 27:2-7) he owes nothing. Since the person is about to be killed he has no “worth”.
(2) As above, the “doomed item” is a person condemned to death. He may not “redeem” himself by paying money to commute his sentence, but rather he must be put to death.
(Regarding Jephthah, although almost all the commentators do not understand that he literally killed his daughter (see this past response), there is one interpretation that he did. The commentator Ramban (Nachmanides) explains that Jephthah erred in his interpretation of this verse, thinking that the law that a doomed person must be put to death extends even to decrees made by a ruler and even though his daughter did no wrong.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: World to Come not Mentioned in the Torah
questions.question: If the belief in the World to Come is so central to Judaism, why does the Torah never mention it?

answers.text:
Thank you for your important question. You are right that it at first strikes us as strange that so fundamental a Jewish belief is not found in the Torah. In fact, the Torah appears to promise us only bounty in this world if we listen to God. See for example Deuteronomy 11:13-15 (from the second paragraph of the Shema):
“And it will be if you surely listen to My commandments… And I will give you the rain of your land in its time, the fall rains and the spring rains, and you will gather your grain, wine, and oil…”
If we will actually receive the infinitely higher rewards of the World to Come, why in the world does the Torah promise us nothing more than bountiful crops – as well as peace, children, and military success? These are no small matters, to be sure, but don’t they utterly pale before the ultimate bliss of a relationship with God in the Hereafter?
The truth is, when we think about it, there are very many basic principles of Judaism which are not really discussed in the Torah either – topics such as God’s omniscience, the function of the angels, the role of Satan, the eternality of the soul, the Resurrection, the existence of God’s Heavenly tribunal, or who God really is at all for that matter.
To be sure, many such issues are alluded to by various verses scattered throughout the Torah, and if one combs the Torah carefully he can gain a fairly good understanding of many areas of Jewish philosophy. But one thing is clear: The Torah is not a work of theology. It does not set out to write an orderly treatise on Judaism’s beliefs. Key philosophical issues can at best be inferred from passing verses, but that is about it.
The reason for this is because God had an entirely different purpose in writing and giving us the Torah, as we’ll see below. And when we understand that purpose, we will see that the questions of what are and are not included do not even begin.
Before I go on, I’ll mention that the Talmud does spend a few pages listing allusions to the World to Come in the Torah (Sanhedrin 90-91). Apart from that, there are a number of important additional verses we should be aware of:
(1) I Samuel 28:7-19: The episode in which King Saul has a necromancer call up the soul of Samuel.
(2) Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) 3:21: “Who knows that the spirit of men rises upwards [after death] while the spirit of the animal descends downwards towards the earth.”
(3) Kohelet 12:7: “The dust will return to the ground as it was, and the spirit will return to the God who gave it.”
(4) Nehemiah 9:5: “And the Levites said… rise up and bless the Lord your God from the world to the world….”
(5) Isaiah 26:19: “May Your dead live; may my dead bodies rise. Awake and sing, those who dwell in the earth, for Your dew is the dew of lights…”
(6) Daniel 12:2: “Many of those who sleep in the ground will rise, some to eternal life, and some to shame, to everlasting abhorrence.”
These verses make it clear that there is a world beyond this one and that the soul returns to God to live in a different world after death. (See also many examples of righteous individuals being “gathered in to their people” after death, such as Genesis 25:8 and 35:29.) The final two verses above make mention of the Resurrection, with the final referring to the Final Judgment after.
Secondly, in addition to the written Torah, God gave Moses an Oral Law, which further elucidates the written Torah and discusses many subjects not mentioned in it. (This is clear from the Torah itself, which mentions many laws which would impossible to understand and practice if not for the further elaboration of the Oral Law. See e.g. this past response.)
The existence of the World to Come is not only discussed openly in the Oral Torah. It is considered one of the fundamentals of the Jewish faith (Mishna Sanhedrin 10:1). See for example Pirkei Avot (4:16): “This world is only as an entranceway before the World to Come.” Also: “One moment of spiritual bliss in the World to Come is greater than the entire life of this world” (4:17).
Thus, to us, the question is not that perhaps Judaism does not believe in a World to Come. It is as much a part of our tradition as the story of the Exodus. The question is rather why the written Torah, and in particular the Five Books of Moses, chose to make virtually no mention of it.
Many explain along the lines of what we wrote above – that the Torah is clearly not a work on theology – a subject it all but ignores. It is rather God’s “user’s guide” for living well in this world. The Torah is God’s set of instructions for living healthy, fulfilling lives in this world. And if we do so, promises the Torah, this world will be perfected and function in harmony with man – the rains will come in their time, the crops will grow, and mankind will live in peace.
Of course much greater rewards await us in the Next World. But that is not the Torah’s topic. It left the philosophy for the Oral Torah. What it does teach us is how to successfully operate this world. And if we obey God’s will, not only we will be personally happy, but the world itself will function in complete harmony with man – becoming a reflection of the God who created it.
See also these articles which discuss related topics:
And see these two article for a much deeper treatment of this entire topic:
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: The Creation of Man and the Animals
questions.question: In our weekly Torah study session, the question came up why the Torah makes special mention of God’s blowing a soul into Adam after creating him (Genesis 2:7). The animals are living beings as well but their bodies and souls seem to have been created together: as soon as the body was created it seems to have been alive. Why by man was the addition of his soul a separate step?

answers.text:
Thank you for sharing the good inference and I wish your study group much success.
The reason for this is because there is a fundamental difference between human and animal souls. Animals have souls, but they are inherently physical – the life force which animates their bodies. This is what the Sages refer to as the “nefesh”.
Human beings have a nefesh as well, but they have a much higher soul as well – the neshama. This is not a part of the physical world at all, but was breathed into man directly from God’s essence. It likewise had to be specially inserted into Adam’s body after its creation. In fact, the Jewish thinkers explain that one of the miracles of creation is that so lofty an entity as the human soul can be made to (at least partially) reside in a lowly, physical body (see Rashi to Talmud Brachot 60b). This human soul is what gives man his Divine essence, his drive for spirituality, and his free will.
(There are actually three primary levels to the human soul. You can see a more thorough treatment of this topic here.)
This is also implied by the spelling of the Hebrew word used in man’s creation. When God created the animals, the Torah states “va’yi’tzer” – “and He created” (2:19), while by man’s creation (2:7) the same word is used, but with two of the letter yud in the middle syllable instead of one, more like “va’yee’tzer”. The Midrash notes this slight discrepancy and explain that two acts of creation were done – “one creation for this world and one creation for the World to Come” (Bereishit Rabbah 14:5, compare to Rashi to that verse). In other words, unlike the animals, man has an eternal soul which remains alive after his body perishes, and if it is worthy, will enter the eternal life of the World to Come.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Elijah’s Ascent to Heaven
questions.question: I’m trying to understand what exactly occurred when Elijah was taken up in a fiery chariot (II Kings 2:11). The Torah states that he was taken up to Heaven in a whirlwind. Was this a form of death? Elijah is mentioned later in the Torah – that he will come to the people before the arrival of the Messiah, so it seems that he is still alive in some form.

answers.text:
Thank you for raising the interesting issue. According to the Sages, Elijah the Prophet (Eliyahu HaNavi in Hebrew) did not die in the incident, but ascended to Heaven alive (see Talmud Baba Batra 121b, Mo’ed Katan 26a). He was one of very few to have perfected himself to such a degree that he was permitted to enter Heaven during his lifetime. (The other known example is Enoch, great-grandfather of Noah – see Genesis 5:4).) As a result, Elijah became part human and part angel. (See for example Talmud Brachot 4b that he flies more slowly than other angels – presumably because he is part physical (Maharsha there).)
One of the commentators explains that the chariot of fire represented that Elijah’s body (in its original physical state) was consumed, and he thus assumed angelic form when he ascended to Heaven (Radak to II Kings 2:11). Alternatively, the fire separated the spiritual and physical sides of Elijah into two separate parts. He could thus ascend to Heaven as a spiritual being, while his body remaining separate – as a “garment” he could put back on whenever he would need to assume physical form (Malbim there).
As a result, Elijah is alive today, living as an angel in Heaven yet regularly visiting Earth in human form to meet with people and to carry out missions. The Talmud, as well as later Jewish tradition, contains literally hundreds of stories of Elijah visiting great rabbis (many on a regular basis) or disguising himself as an ordinary human (such as a palace guard) and using his assumed identity to intercede with non-Jewish authorities and the like. (See e.g. Talmud Brachot 3a, 29b, Shabbat 33b, Yoma 19b, Ta’anit 22a, etc.) Occasionally Elijah would bring other righteous people with him on visits to Heaven (Baba Metziah 85b, 114a).
There is further a tradition that Elijah will come one day to resolve all doubts we have in Jewish law. The Sages have a common expression that an item whose status cannot be resolved (such as a lost item whose owner cannot be located) “shall rest until Elijah comes” (e.g. Mishna Bava Metziah 1:8, 2:8). (This in particular relates to ruling on situations where we lack information (such as here, the identity of the object's owner). Matters of Jewish law proper are in the hands of the courts to decide.)
The most famous appearance Elijah will make, God willing, will be the one you mentioned. The prophet Malachi, in the final prophecy of all the books of the Prophets, states (3:23-24): “Behold I will send to you Elijah the Prophet, before the coming the great and awesome day of the Lord. And he will bring back the hearts of the fathers to the sons, and the hearts of the sons to their fathers…”
Shortly before the Messiah’s arrival and the great battles of the End of Days, Elijah will come. He will warn us of the upcoming Armageddon, and help bring us to unity and to repentance, in order that we are spared the suffering and live to merit the Redemption.
There are a few rituals which Elijah is particularly associated with today. One is a circumcision (brit milah), in which we set up a special chair for Elijah (“Kisei Shel Eliyahu”). The second is the Passover Seder, in which the “cup of Elijah” is poured towards the end of the evening, when we open our doors and ask God to bring the Final Redemption. According to one opinion in the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 11b), the redemption will occur in the month of Nissan, when Passover falls. We likewise open our doors in anticipation of Elijah’s arrival to herald the wondrous event.
(There doesn’t seem to be a source for what I and many learned in first grade – that if you look very closely at the cup, you’ll see it go down a tiny sip when Eliyahu visits – although it’s not hard to imagine you saw it.)
It’s possible to suggest a connection between these two events. Circumcision represents that we see ourselves as God’s special people, different from the nations of the world. Every time a new baby is born and circumcised, we further assert that we are a separate people. Because we have maintained our identity, God will one day recognize us as His own nation and redeem us. Elijah is invited to every circumcision to witness the devotion we have to maintaining our identity and tradition. And as a result, we can be confident that he will visit us at the Seder one year to proclaim to us the imminent arrival of the Messiah.
May the Messiah come speedily in our days!
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Are Religious People Happy?
questions.question: I grew up Orthodox but fell out of practice in my early 20s. In the few years since then I have dabbled with several other religious beliefs or just secular living, and I never really felt fulfilled. At this point, I’m finding myself slowly drawn back towards Orthodoxy. But one basic issue is bothering me. Growing up, I was never turned on to the Orthodox lifestyle.
